query: The Pigeons Are on Strike {The loft's message pigeons are on strike. They sit on the rafter in a row, puffed and silent, beside a list of demands scratched in claw-marks.|The pigeons have struck again. The demands have grown: better grain, a window that shuts, and the removal of a particular courier.|The pigeons are on strike. They look at you as you come in, as if you've been appointed to negotiate.} {The undelivered notes are piling up.|One pigeon is plainly the ringleader; it has a bald patch and a stare.|{season == "winter": The window that doesn't shut is letting the snow in, which seems fair.|Every courier in the loft is pretending not to be afraid of the ringleader.}} Talk the ringleader round {You offer seed, flattery and a promise about the window. The ringleader considers, coos once, and the strike is over.|You talk to the ringleader as you'd talk to a magistrate. It accepts your terms and a raisin.|The ringleader hears you out, eye to eye. The pigeons rise in a clatter and the backlog flies.} {The ringleader hears your offer and pecks your knuckle, hard. Talks have broken down.|The whole rafter turns its back on you, in unison, which is very hard to recover from. One of them nips your ear on the way.|They accept the raisin and refuse the terms. One of them sits on your head, claws first, to make the point.} Carry their notes by hand {You run the undelivered notes round the castle yourself, all seven towers, and come back with sore legs and the pigeons' quiet contempt.|You deliver the notes on foot. The pigeons watch you go, smug as landladies. Your feet ache by the last tower.|You run the round on foot again. You're faster than a pigeon on the stairs, if not in the air, and your calves know it.}
